sections.title: Sound of the letter
paragraphs: The letter is called (Ypsilon) /ʏpsilɔn/. Its main sound appears in (Yoga) /ˈjoːɡa/, which means a Hindu spiritual practice. This letter has four sounds in German. Most of its words come from other tongues. Listen to how each word sounds in speech.

sections.title: How to say it
paragraphs: For the first sound, place your tongue high and front, push your lips forward, and keep them in a tight circle. For the second sound, lower your tongue slightly and keep your lips loose. For the third sound, raise the middle of your tongue near the hard roof of the mouth and glide into the vowel. For the fourth sound, spread your lips and raise your tongue high. Touch your throat to feel your voice buzz for each one.

sections.title: Spelling rules
paragraphs: In stressed open beats of words from Greek, the letter makes a long vowel, as in (Typ) /tyːp/. In closed beats of Greek words, it makes a short vowel, as in (System) /zʏsˈteːm/. Before other vowels in newer borrowed words, it sounds like a consonant, as in (Yacht) /jaxt/. At the end of words or in weak beats, it sounds like a short vowel, as in (Handy) /ˈhɛndi/.

sections.title: Mistakes to avoid
paragraphs: Do not replace the vowel with the one in the English word boot. That English sound pulls the tongue back. Instead, push your tongue forward as if saying the vowel in see, then make a small circle with your lips. Also, do not turn the vowel into a diphthong like the one in English my.
